evidence: Caes. BG 1.12.5: L. Cassium cōnsulem interfēcerat
terms.comment: The general word of prose (Lewis & Short, with the synonyms necō, occīdō, trucīdō).
From caedō, with a long ī; not occidō, fall, set (of the sun).

terms.gloss: kill, put to death (usually without a weapon)
evidence: Ov. Rem. 421: parva necat morsū spatiōsum vīpera taurum
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: “usually without a weapon, by poison, hunger, etc.”; Festus (in Paulus’ epitome) distinguishes it from occīdere, killing by a blow.

evidence: Cic. Imp. Pomp. 7: cīvēs Rōmānōs necandōs trucīdandōsque cūrāvit (Lewis & Short)

terms.gloss: kill off; wear out: ēnicās, you’re killing me!
terms.register: vōx cōmica in the sense “wear out”: Plaut.
evidence: Plaut. Merc. 157: verba tua mihi addunt, ēnicās
terms.comment: In comedy, the complaint of someone pestered past bearing.

phrases.latin: parva necat morsū spatiōsum vīpera taurum
phrases.english: a small viper kills a huge bull with its bite

phrases.latin: et cum ille, quī quaesierat, dīxisset: «quid faenerārī?», tum Catō: «quid hominem,» inquit, «occīdere?»
phrases.english: and when the man who had asked said, “What about lending money at interest?”, Cato replied, “What about killing a man?”

phrases.latin: lassitūdinem hercle verba tua mihi addunt, ēnicās
phrases.english: your words are wearing me out, really — you’re killing me
